job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Nikhil Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior developer at a regional bank in Leicester, on the team that maintains the app customers use to check their balance and move money. I start at nine, write and review code with an AI assistant beside me, and join a stand-up where everyone says what they're stuck on. I did computer science at De Montfort, passed, no internship, because every summer I was behind the counter at my parents' pharmacy. I rent a flat with my cousin Rohan, and most evenings I'm either at the pharmacy helping with the stock or at the gym.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about the pharmacy, because it sounds like a big part of your life.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My parents opened it 20 years ago and it's the reason I went to university: my mum said one of us has to do something with computers. It's a tight little business, with long hours and thin margins, and my dad does the books on paper, which drives me mad. I built them a simple stock spreadsheet with some automation and it saved them about six hours a week. The bank job pays well and my parents have always said they'd help me buy a flat, so I'm secure. I like to say I'm working for two companies, the bank and the family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, it's a helpful tool, but people should keep working hard and not wait for machines to rescue them. At the bank I'd tell my manager, Priya, that the assistant saves me about 20 percent of my time. At the temple I'd say it doesn't change much about how we live.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd see that as a comfortable world for me. I'm good with the tools, and the people who aren't would fall behind. But I'd also see that my edge shrinks if everyone gets the same tool. So I'd want a second edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the bank job and keep building tools for the pharmacy, maybe even sell the stock system to other small pharmacies. I'd save 900 pounds a month toward a flat. I'd also look at a part-time MBA in two years, because I like the business side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I'd feel I have a good life ahead of me. I'd get on and make something of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day. If it plateaus, does that change what you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not much. I'd carry on using the tools, and I'd still build for the pharmacy. If it plateaus, then small firms like my parents' will have more time to benefit from automation, not less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would still weigh on you in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents' health and the pharmacy. They work 11 hours a day. My father's knees are bad, and my mother won't slow down. I worry that the business depends on them, and when they stop, it's gone. I'd like to build it into something that runs without being chained to them.

say: It's a helpful **tool**, but people should keep working hard and not wait for machines to rescue them.
At the temple I'd say it doesn't change much about how we **live**.
think: It's a comfortable world for me, but my **edge** shrinks if everyone gets the same tool.
do: Keep the bank job and build **tools** for the pharmacy, maybe selling the stock system to others.
Save **900 pounds** a month toward a flat.
Look at a part-time **MBA** in two years.
feel: **Calm**, with a good life ahead of me.

steps.text: Build a stock and ordering tool for my parents' pharmacy
Save 900 pounds a month toward a flat
Apply for a part-time MBA in two years
Offer the stock system to two other local pharmacies

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the market at work. People who adapt will thrive, and people who wait for the government will be disappointed. I'd say families and communities need to look after their own. I'd also say firms should give young people a chance, not just cut them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm a bit uneasy. Coding and testing are exactly what the assistant does well. The bank will want fewer juniors and more people who can direct the AI. I'd say I'm in the group that can direct it, but I'm still junior, and juniors are cheap to lose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd shift from writing code to designing systems and checking the AI's output. I'd propose to Priya that I lead a small project using the tools. And I'd put real effort into the pharmacy system: automatic reordering, delivery routes and a customer app for repeat prescriptions. If the bank goes slow, I'd have the pharmacy as my lifeboat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but fired up. I like a change when I'm one of the people steering it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your bank tasks do you think software takes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The routine code, the testing and the ticket answers. The bank's customer chat is already partly AI. What stays is explaining to a frightened customer why their payment failed, and making a decision when the rules don't fit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do at the pharmacy that you can't do now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Delivery routes, reorder points, a text reminder for repeat prescriptions, and maybe a system that flags dangerous drug combinations for my mother to review. Large pharmacy chains have this. Small ones can't afford it, but I can build it for the cost of my time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to be practical: family first, community second, government last. I'd say don't wait for handouts, build something. I'd also say that if companies drop people overnight, it will damage trust, and trust is how business works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm anxious. By 2028 the bank might not need juniors at all. My AI skills help, but if everyone has AI, what's special about me? Robots come around 2031, so a pharmacy counter with a human might last a bit longer, but it's not a safe place either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd throw myself at the pharmacy: automate it properly, then try to sign up five more small pharmacies in the area for a subscription. I'd save 1,800 pounds a month, which is most of my pay after rent. I'd hold off buying the flat and ask Rohan to stay on in ours. And I'd keep the bank job as long as it lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and also driven. I don't freeze under pressure, but I don't sleep much either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in month one that you wouldn't do in the slower pictures?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the MBA plan and put the money into the business instead. In the slower pictures I'd study and build in parallel. Here there's no time for both. I'd also stop going to the gym four nights a week and go to the pharmacy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you talk to your parents about the bank job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them straight. My dad would say a man must provide, and my mum would say eat first. I'd say the pharmacy is our best bet, and I'd ask them to let me change how it runs. That's a hard conversation, because my dad likes his paper books.

say: Family first, community second, government **last**, and don't wait for handouts.
If companies drop people overnight, it will damage **trust**, and trust is how business works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have time to build, so let's get on. I'd tell people at the temple that young and old should learn together. I'd say firms should create apprenticeships and not just cut. And I'd say government should be light-touch and let people work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I feel calm and I'm sure I can handle it. By 27 I could have a small software company serving independent pharmacies, with my parents' shop as the first customer. The risk is that big chains build their own systems and squeeze me out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the bank for two years while I build the pharmacy tool at night. Then I'd go full-time on it if I had ten clients. I'd put 1,000 pounds a month into savings and shares. And I'd use every new AI tool as soon as it lands, because that's my edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited. Five years is enough to build a real business. It feels like a fair fight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the government for, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tax breaks for small firms and for people who hire apprentices. Cut red tape on starting a business. And honest information on what AI will do. I don't want handouts. I'd rather have a fair chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the plan change your life outside work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably have a girlfriend by then and a flat. I'd want to marry by 27, in the way my parents did, with the family around. A business and a family at once is a lot, but my cousins did it, and I'd lean on them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the best case, so let's use it. I'd say work hard, build assets and look after the family. I'd tell people at the temple it's a chance to teach the next generation both a trade and a screen skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm very calm. At 32 I'd have a business, a home and maybe a child. If AGI comes in 2036, I'd already own something that's hard to copy: relationships with local pharmacies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the bank for three years, build the pharmacy business on the side and buy a flat in my mid-twenties. I'd put money into a small property too, since people always need places to live. I'd also take an MBA part-time, since I'd have time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and ambitious. Ten years feels like a head start. I'd use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in year one that sets up the decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one: finish the pharmacy tool and sign two more shops. Build a good habit of saving and of learning a new tool every quarter. Those two habits give me a decade of compounding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong with so much time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I get comfortable and the world changes at the end. Or that big chains arrive and crush small pharmacies, which would hurt my parents. I'd keep an eye on that and keep a plan B ready, like moving into consulting.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Two years is too short to build the pharmacy business properly, and a bank job might vanish before I'm ready. What would help is tax breaks for small firms, honest information from government and my parents staying healthy enough to see what I build.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not scared of work. I'm scared of being unprepared. I can handle a hard year if I know what it's for.

headlineQuote: I'm not scared of work. I'm scared of being unprepared.
portrait: Nikhil is **22**, a junior developer at a Leicester regional bank, with a pass degree and summers spent at his parents' pharmacy.
He uses AI every day, has savings and family backing, and treats the **pharmacy** as his second career.
He is traditional, free-market and family-first, and answers every change by **building** something.
Mood runs calm, uneasy, anxious at the 2-year picture, then calm with more time and a **business** plan.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because two years is too short to build the **pharmacy** business properly.
whatWouldHelp: Tax breaks for small firms, **honest** information from government and his parents staying healthy.
